extracted.intended_audience: NSF proposers (PIs), authorized organizational representatives (AORs), research administrators, external reviewers/panelists, and NSF program staff
extracted.subtask_short: NSF proposal merit review and processing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing, submitting, reviewing, and administratively processing NSF proposals under the PAPPG, including merit review principles and criteria, reviewer selection, file updates, revisions during review, funding recommendation, award/decline decisions, appeal procedures, and disclosure of proposal materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Principle — highest quality and potential to advance knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: All NSF projects should be of the highest quality and have the potential to advance, if not transform, the frontiers of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle must be given due diligence by PIs and organizations when preparing proposals, by reviewers when evaluating proposals, and by NSF staff when recommending proposals for funding and overseeing awards. It signals expectation of rigorous, high-quality research or education activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Principle — contribution to societal goals (Broader Impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF projects, in the aggregate, should contribute more broadly to achieving societal goals. These broader impacts may be accomplished through the research itself, through activities that are directly related to specific research projects, or through activities that are supported by, but are complementary to, the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project activities may be based on established or innovative methods but must be well justified. PIs should describe how proposed activities contribute to societal goals (e.g., education, workforce development, public engagement, infrastructure) and justify their approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Principle — meaningful assessment and PI accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful assessment and evaluation of NSF funded projects should be based on appropriate metrics, keeping in mind the likely correlation between the effect of broader impacts and the resources provided to implement projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small activities may not be meaningfully evaluated in isolation; assessment may be more appropriate at an aggregated level. Nonetheless, PIs are expected to be accountable: individual projects should include clearly stated goals, specific descriptions of intended activities, and a plan to document outputs and to assess success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Criterion — Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The Intellectual Merit criterion encompasses the potential to advance knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual Merit is one of two National Science Board–approved merit review criteria and must be given full consideration. Reviewers should consider the project's potential to advance knowledge within its field or across fields, creativity/originality, and the rigor of the research approach. Intellectual Merit alone is necessary but not sufficient for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit Review Criterion — Broader Impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Broader Impacts criterion encompasses the potential to benefit society and contribute to the achievement of specific, desired societal outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broader Impacts is the second NSB-approved criterion and must be given full consideration alongside Intellectual Merit. Consider how project activities will benefit society (e.g., through education, broadening participation, outreach, partnerships). Broader Impacts alone is necessary but not sufficient for funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to be considered in review for both criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating NSF proposals, reviewers will be asked to consider what the proposers want to do, why they want to do it, how they plan to do it, how they will know if they succeed, and what benefits could accrue if the project is successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific review questions to apply to both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts: (1) What is the potential to advance knowledge (Intellectual Merit) or benefit society (Broader Impacts)? (2) To what extent do the proposed activities suggest and explore creative, original, or potentially transformative concepts? (3) Is the plan well-reasoned, well-organized, and based on a sound rationale, and does it incorporate a mechanism to assess success? (4) How well qualified is the individual, team, or organization? (5) Are there adequate resources (institutional or collaborative) available to carry out the activities?

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction — both criteria must be fully addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Both criteria are to be given full consideration during the review and decision-making processes; each criterion is necessary but neither, by itself, is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposers must fully address both Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts in their Project Description. Reviewers are strongly encouraged to review the criteria (including related guidance in Chapter II) before evaluating proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of Reviewers — required reviewer qualifications and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should have special knowledge of the science and engineering subfields involved and, within reasonable limits, complementary specialties; broader or generalized knowledge is required for proposals involving substantial size/complexity; broad knowledge of infrastructure and education activities is helpful to evaluate societal contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To the extent possible, review panels should reflect diverse representation (organization type, reviewer diversity, age distribution, geographic balance). For complex/multidisciplinary proposals, include reviewers with broader expertise. Program Officers select reviewers at their discretion and may use proposer suggestions or exclusions as one source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal File Updates — procedural requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations may request replacement of files or revision of proposal attributes via the Submitted Proposals Module in Research.gov. A request must be signed and submitted by the AOR and include a Proposal Update Justification addressing why changes are requested and differences between original and replacement files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automatic acceptance of a file update occurs if submitted prior to the deadline date, prior to initiation of external peer review when a target date is used, or prior to initiation of external peer review for unsolicited proposals. Requests after those timeframes require acceptance by the cognizant Program Officer and should be submitted only to correct technical problems (formatting/printing). Changes in content should not be requested after stated timeframes. Only one request per proposal will be considered at a time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisions to proposals during the review process — significant developments and negotiation constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: If a significant development arises that might materially affect review, the proposer must contact the cognizant Program Officer; submitting additional information must not be used to circumvent page limits or deadlines. Program Officers may engage in discussions with PIs before recommending support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget negotiations may involve changing total support or specific budget items; Program Officers may suggest reducing/eliminating costs that are clearly unnecessary or unreasonable, generally excluding faculty salaries, salary rates, fringe benefits, or tuition. Indirect cost (F&A) rates are not negotiable. Program Officers may discuss 'bottom line' award amounts but may not renegotiate cost sharing or organizational commitments. When budget reductions are 10% or more, a corresponding reduction in project scope is expected and proposers must submit a revised budget, budget justification, and a Budget Impact Statement describing the impact; revisions must be submitted via Research.gov and signed by the AOR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding recommendation process and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: After review and consideration of scientific, technical, and programmatic factors, the cognizant NSF Program Officer recommends to the Division Director whether a proposal should be declined or recommended for award. Senior NSF staff further review recommendations for awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review and consideration process may take up to six months due to volume; complex proposals may take longer. If recommended for award, the PI may be contacted to assist in preparing the public award abstract and title. A Program Officer's recommendation does not constitute approval or obligation of Federal funds; only an appointed Grants and Agreements Officer may make commitments or obligate funds. PIs and organizations should not infer commitments from discussions with Program Officers and should avoid making financial/personnel commitments prior to an award notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: NSF decision to award or decline — pre-award review and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: If programmatic approval is obtained, the recommended proposal goes to the Division of Grants and Agreements (DGA) or Division of Acquisition and Cooperative Support (DACS) for review of business, financial, and policy implications, including use of NSF’s risk-based framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DGA generally makes the decision to award or decline within 30 days after the program Division/Office recommendation. DACS review of major facilities follows the Research Infrastructure Guide. Proposals from organizations with no active NSF award in the preceding five years, proposals involving special coordination, cooperative agreements, proposals or renewals exceeding $20 million, or other unusual considerations may require additional processing time. Declinations that meet OMB reporting guidelines may be reported to the designated integrity and performance system after appeal procedures are exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process to appeal NSF’s decision to decline for financial/administrative reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposer declined for financial or administrative reasons may first discuss the decision with the cognizant Grants and Agreements Officer or Branch Chief. If dissatisfied, the organization's AOR may submit a request for review to the cognizant Division Director of DGA or DACS within 30 days of the declination notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The request need not follow a prescribed format but must include a full statement of the proposer's position, facts and reasons supporting that the declination was unwarranted, and may include supporting documentation that was available at the time of decision. NSF will not consider new information that would not have been available at the time of decision (e.g., new financial stability info). The reviewing official(s) will not include individuals involved in the decline decision, may request additional information limited to what was available at the time, and will forward a report within 30 days of NSF’s receipt of the request; the Division Director (or designee) will normally communicate a final written decision within 15 days of receipt of the report. The Division Director's decision is final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review information provided to PI after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: When a decision (award or declination) has been made, NSF releases to the PI: a description of the review process used; copies of all reviews used in the decision (with reviewer-identifying information redacted); panel summaries and recommendations if applicable; and site-visit reports if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not provided in the panel summary, the PI receives a written explanation of the basis for declination. PIs may request other releasable materials in NSF's file on the proposal. Everything in the file is usually releasable to the PI except information that identifies reviewers or other pending/declined proposals. Reviews are provided to give feedback to improve proposed research and methods and to assist in future proposal preparation; they are not intended for other purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release of recipient proposal information to public (FOIA and confidentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal that results in an NSF award will be made available to the public on request, consistent with the Freedom of Information Act, except for privileged, personal, proprietary, or otherwise legally exempt information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate labeling in proposals aids identification of exempt material. Such information will be withheld from public disclosure to the extent permitted by law. Portions describing inventions in which the Government or recipient has rights will not normally be made public until a reasonable time has been allowed for filing patent applications. NSF will notify recipients of requests for copies of funded proposals so recipients may advise NSF of inventions or other confidential/commercial information described.
